editorial_plan.report_thesis: The report maps technology and media change across user attention, services, content, and distribution, while examining revenue capture and gaps across industry layers as strategic questions.

themes.theme: Competitive positioning across the unified industry stack
Television transition and the smart-cable proposition

toc_entries.section_title: The 9 most important insights for tech and media in 2016
toc_entries.display_title: The 9 most important insights for tech and media in 2016
toc_entries.summary: An opening overview lists the report’s nine central insights, from attention and messaging through consumer-tech revenue and competition across industry layers.
key_points: The listed insights address attention, messaging, streaming audio, cord cutting, and the future of pay television.
The remaining topics cover eSports and wagering, app-store economics, revenue capture, and predicting competitive moves.

toc_entries.summary: This section examines how people allocate attention across media and digital activities, and how businesses can grow by capturing user time. It argues that attention capture is not a zero-sum contest.
key_points: The report says a billion-dollar business can be built by capturing less than a minute of an average user’s daily attention (p. 10).
For U.S. users aged 18+, the chart’s 2011–2017E CAGRs are video 4.5%, audio 4.9%, social media 17.8%, and gaming 11.9% (p. 12).
The report identifies a concentration of user time among a few digital properties and platforms (p. 9).

toc_entries.summary: The section describes messaging as an expanding media activity and a platform for new services and revenue streams. It compares the scale and monetization of messaging services and considers consumer and enterprise uses.
key_points: Activate forecasts 1.1 billion additional messaging users by 2018; the chart shows 3.6 billion messaging users, 2.4 billion social-media users, and 4.0 billion internet users in 2018E (p. 16).
The report points to WeChat, KakaoTalk, and LINE as examples of messaging platforms with broader services and higher ARPU than the global services shown in the comparison (p. 33).
It describes app and bot integrations as a way messaging can add functions such as search and workplace productivity (p. 31).
The section outlines potential messaging uses including news, shopping, mobile web, productivity, games, finance, education, sports, health, and business (p. 32).

toc_entries.summary: This section assesses the audio market, where streaming competes with established listening formats, and discusses curation and podcast advertising as areas of opportunity.
key_points: The U.S. audio-consumption chart for users aged 13+ reports a total of 4 hours 5 minutes in 2014; AM/FM accounts for 52%, while streaming accounts for about 12% (pp. 35–36).
The report presents human curation and algorithmic recommendations as distinct approaches to differentiation, with Beats 1 and Spotify’s Discover Weekly as examples (p. 47).
Podcast examples and standard ad placements are used to show that podcasts can command premium advertising rates (p. 55).

toc_entries.summary: The section argues that the shift away from traditional television is gradual, even as viewing habits diversify beyond appointment television. It emphasizes the continued importance of TV- and studio-produced programming.
key_points: The report states that changes in television are not simply a technology transition and that cord cutting will not happen overnight (p. 65).
Its U.S. monthly video-consumption chart says people still spend most of their time with TV- and studio-produced content (p. 67).
The section describes audiences forming around content beyond traditional appointment viewing, including on-demand and creator-driven formats (p. 72).

toc_entries.summary: This section examines what a viable challenger to cable would need to offer, and why incumbent operators have structural advantages. Its central argument is that the likely “cable killer” is a higher-end “smart cable” experience rather than simply a low-priced competitor.
key_points: The report defines a potential cable killer as combining equivalent or better video content, a lower-cost package, and a better user experience and reliability (p. 86).
It says a new entrant would have to begin by licensing top-tier content (p. 87).
Cable operators benefit from economies of scale that lower their programming costs per subscriber (p. 88).
The proposed “smart cable” approach targets lucrative customers with a superior high-end experience rather than competing only on low price (p. 91).

toc_entries.summary: This section describes the expansion of gaming into advertising, eSports, and wagering. It presents eSports as a growing spectator business and skill-based wagering as an additional way to monetize game audiences.
key_points: The report’s global entertainment-spending chart lists video gaming at $74 billion in 2014 and frames advertising and gambling as potential expansion streams (p. 95).

The “Activate Forecast: eSports Revenue, Global, 2018E” chart forecasts a $4 billion business, with $2.2 billion in APAC, $1.3 billion in North America, $0.4 billion in Europe, and $0.1 billion in Latin America (p. 104).
The Dota 2 tournament prize-pool chart gives $2 million for 2012, $3 million for 2013, $11 million for 2014, and $18 million for 2015, and labels the period’s CAGR as 126% (p. 102).
The report characterizes wagering as a real-money layer that is skill-based and social, and identifies multiplayer games and eSports events as likely settings (p. 106).

toc_entries.summary: This section considers business models built around app-store distribution and engagement, while distinguishing those roles from monetization.
key_points: The report describes a new wave of companies using the app store for distribution and engagement, but not monetization (p. 123).
The section’s framing cautions that building a business around an app-store presence does not itself mean capturing the revenue (p. 115).

toc_entries.summary: This section compares annual average revenue per user across consumer technology and media companies in the United States and globally. It highlights differences in revenue levels and year-over-year growth, while identifying U.S. pay-TV providers as the highest-ARPU group in the U.S. comparison.
key_points: For the U.S. 2014 comparison, the report states that pay-TV providers continue to capture the highest average revenue per user (p. 125).
The global 2014 chart compares annual ARPU and 2013–2014 ARPU growth across consumer technology and media companies (p. 126).
The section notes that ARPU calculations use consolidated U.S. or global revenues, with specific company-level exclusions and definitions disclosed beneath the charts (pp. 125–126).

toc_entries.summary: The final insight maps technology and media businesses as an increasingly unified stack of channels, products, services, and content layers. It argues that gaps in the stack can help anticipate strategic moves and future M&A.
key_points: The stack diagram groups layers from connectivity and delivery through devices, platforms, services, distribution, and original content (p. 128).
The report uses the independent players in each layer to identify where major companies may have gaps (p. 129).
It expects the next wave of M&A activity to be driven by larger players filling gaps with independent players (p. 131).
The section’s conclusion is that identifying missing layers can help anticipate the next strategic moves of major consumer technology and media players (p. 130).

toc_entries.section_title: Activate: We are the leading strategy consulting firm for technology, media, entertainment and information companies
toc_entries.summary: The closing page describes Activate’s consulting work with senior leaders and investors, including growth strategy, digital strategy, new businesses and products, pricing, sales and marketing effectiveness, and strategic diligence.
key_points: Activate says it works with CEOs, senior management teams, and principal investors to drive growth and position companies to win.
Its listed services include growth strategy, digital strategy, new businesses and products, pricing, sales and marketing effectiveness, and strategic due diligence.

For U.S. users aged 18+, the 2011–2017E CAGRs for time spent were video 4.5%, audio 4.9%, social media 17.8%, and gaming 11.9%. The report says a new wave of companies are using the app store for distribution and engagement, but not monetization.

expert_comment: The report forecasts messaging will add 1.1 billion new users by 2018. Separately, it says a new wave of companies use app stores for distribution and engagement, but not monetization; for Slack, third-party integrations and automated bots function like an app store, differentiate Slack from competitors, and are essential for adoption. MarketLense would assess monetization separately from user-growth and adoption propositions when evaluating these opportunities.

report_vs/artifacts/expert_comment.public_output: The report forecasts messaging will add 1.1 billion new users by 2018. Separately, it says a new wave of companies use app stores for distribution and engagement, but not monetization; for Slack, third-party integrations and automated bots function like an app store, differentiate Slack from competitors, and are essential for adoption. Taken together, these findings make user growth, adoption functionality, and monetization distinct strategic considerations. MarketLense would assess monetization separately from user-growth and adoption propositions when evaluating these opportunities.
